q: A patient has a $1,500 deductible, 20 percent coinsurance and has already paid $1,500 toward the deductible. A covered bill is $1,000. How much does the patient owe?
r: 20 percent of $1,000, since the deductible is already met.
w: $1,000, because the patient must pay the whole of any bill until the plan year ends
$800, which is the share of the bill that the insurance plan will pay for the patient
$1,700, found by adding the deductible to the coinsurance amount for the bill

q: A plan pays 80 percent of an allowed amount of $500 after the deductible is met. How much does the insurer pay?
r: 80 percent of $500.
w: $100, which is the share of the bill that the patient pays under the coinsurance term
$500, which is the whole allowed amount that the plan would pay if there were no coinsurance
$80, found by treating the percentage as a flat dollar amount for the claim

q: A provider bills $300 but the insurer's allowed amount is $200. The in-network provider must generally:
r: Write off the $100 difference
Contracted rates limit what can be charged.
w: Bill the patient for the full $100 difference on top of the amount owed under the plan
Bill the insurer again for the $100 until it pays the full amount that was first billed
The allowed amount is the limit.
Cancel the whole claim and refuse to treat the patient from then on

q: What is balance billing?
r: Billing a patient for the difference between the provider's charge and the insurer's allowed amount
Out-of-network providers may do this.
w: Billing the insurer for the full charge and nothing to the patient at any time
Billing the patient for only the copay due at the time of the visit to the clinic
Billing a second insurer for the part of the claim that the first insurer denied

q: A claim is denied because the patient's policy had lapsed. What is the best next step?
r: Verify coverage dates and bill the patient or correct the insurance information
Check for a coverage error first.
w: Resubmit the same claim many times until the insurer pays it without changes
Write off the whole amount without checking anything about the patient's coverage
Change the date of service to a date when the policy was active to get it paid

q: A claim lists a diagnosis code and a procedure code. What does the diagnosis code show?
r: Why the service was needed
It supports medical necessity.
w: How much the service cost to provide to the patient on the date of the visit
Which provider performed the service for the patient at the clinic
Which insurer will pay for the service and what share the patient owes

q: What do CPT codes describe?
r: Procedures and services performed by providers
They are used for billing.
w: Diseases and conditions diagnosed in a patient by the doctor during the visit
The locations of hospital wards and the names of the units in each building
The insurance plans that a patient holds and the dates for which they apply

q: What do ICD-10 codes describe?
r: Diagnoses and conditions
They support medical necessity for services.
w: Procedures and services performed by providers, which are used for billing the payer
Drugs and medicines that are prescribed to patients by a doctor or by a nurse
The prices charged by a hospital for the use of its rooms and equipment

q: What is upcoding?
r: Billing for a more expensive service than was actually provided
It is a form of fraud.
w: Billing for a less expensive service than was provided so the patient pays less
Billing for a service twice to two different payers on the same date of service
Updating a patient's diagnosis codes to match what the doctor wrote in the chart

q: What is unbundling in medical billing?
r: Billing separately for services that should be billed together as one
It raises payment improperly.
w: Combining several unrelated services into one single code to get a lower payment
Splitting a patient's bill into small payments that are due over several months
Sending a bill to a patient and to the insurer at the same time

q: What is a remittance advice (or EOP)?
r: A document from a payer explaining how a claim was paid or adjusted
It lists allowed amounts and denials.
w: A letter sent to a patient that thanks him for choosing the hospital for care
A form a patient signs to agree to treatment before a procedure is carried out
A report that shows how many patients visited the clinic during a given month

q: What is a clean claim?
r: A claim with no errors that can be processed without extra information
It is paid faster.
w: A claim that has been washed of the patient's personal information before it is sent
A claim that the insurer has denied because the form was filled in by hand
A claim for a service that costs nothing to the patient or to the payer

q: What is a timely filing limit?
r: The deadline by which a claim must be submitted to the payer
Late claims may be denied.
w: The time a patient may wait in the waiting room before seeing the doctor
The number of claims that a biller may submit to an insurer in one day
The time that the insurer has to answer a phone call from the provider's office

q: What is coordination of benefits?
r: Determining which insurer pays first when a patient has more than one plan
It prevents duplicate payment.
w: Sending bills to the government only, whatever the patient's insurance may cover
Pooling the premiums of two insurers into one account for the patient to use
Splitting a bill equally among all the doctors who treated the patient

q: A child is covered by both parents' plans. Which plan is usually primary?
r: The plan of the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year
This is the birthday rule.
w: The plan of the parent with the higher pay, whatever the dates of their birthdays
The plan of the older parent, whatever the dates of their birthdays in the year
The plan that charges the lower monthly premium to the family each month

q: What is a copayment?
r: A fixed amount a patient pays for a covered service at the time of care
For example $25 for a visit.
w: The yearly total you pay for insurance, which is billed in equal monthly amounts
The portion of the cost that the insurer will never pay, whatever the policy says
The amount you pay before the plan starts paying for any covered care

q: What is an out-of-pocket maximum?
r: The most a patient pays in a year for covered care
After it is reached, the plan pays 100 percent.
w: The most the insurer will pay in a lifetime for the care of a single patient
The least a patient must pay for a single visit to the doctor's office
The amount a patient pays each month to keep the policy in force

q: What is a premium?
r: The amount paid regularly to keep insurance coverage
It is paid whether or not care is used.
w: The amount a patient pays before the plan starts paying for covered care
The fixed fee a patient pays at each visit to a doctor or clinic
The share of a bill that a patient pays after the deductible is met

q: What is a Health Savings Account (HSA) used for?
r: Saving pre-tax money for qualified medical expenses
It is paired with a high-deductible plan.
w: Paying the premiums of a car insurance policy on the vehicle of the account owner
Saving for retirement in a fund that cannot be used for any health costs
Paying hospital employees their wages out of a special pool of funds

q: What is a flexible spending account (FSA)?
r: An account funded with pre-tax pay to cover eligible health costs
Funds often must be used within the plan year.
w: An account for retirement savings that earns interest and is paid out at age 65
An account that the hospital uses to pay its suppliers for medical goods
An account that holds the money for a patient's premium for the whole of a life

q: What does Medicare Part B mostly cover?
r: Doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive services
It is medical insurance.
w: Hospital inpatient stays and the surgery that is carried out during them
Prescription drugs bought at a pharmacy by the member of the plan
Private plan options that bundle Parts A and B with extra benefits

q: What does Medicare Part A mostly cover?
r: Hospital inpatient stays and related care
It is hospital insurance.
w: Doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive services, paid for by a monthly premium
Prescription drugs bought at a pharmacy by the member of the plan
Dental and vision care for members who have the plan through an employer

q: Who is generally eligible for Medicare?
r: People age 65 or older and some younger people with disabilities
It is a federal program.
w: Only people with low income, regardless of their age or any disability they may have
Only active members of the military and their families, whatever their age
Only employees of hospitals who have worked there for more than ten years

q: What is Medicaid?
r: A joint federal and state program that helps cover health costs for people with low income
Rules vary by state.
w: A federal program for people age 65 or older, funded through payroll taxes
A program for hospital employees only, who pay in a small amount each month
A private insurance plan that is sold by employers to their staff members

q: What is a Preferred Provider Organization (PPO)?
r: A plan that lets members see in-network or out-of-network providers, with lower costs in network
It offers flexibility.
w: A plan that requires members to use one clinic only, with no cover for care elsewhere
That is more like an HMO.
A plan that pays for no care at all until the patient reaches the age of 65
A plan that is run by the government for people who live in rural areas only

q: What is a Health Maintenance Organization (HMO)?
r: A health plan with a network of providers that usually requires referrals for specialists
Out-of-network care is often not covered.
w: A plan that lets members see any provider with no limits, and with no referral needed
That is closer to a PPO.
A plan that pays only for emergencies and for no routine care of any kind
A plan that is available only to people who earn a low income in the state

q: What is prior authorization?
r: Insurer approval required before certain services or drugs are provided
It controls cost and use.
w: A patient's signature after treatment, which proves that the care was received in full
A doctor's note that explains why a patient missed an appointment at the clinic
An approval that the hospital gives itself before it buys a piece of equipment

q: What is a referral authorization?
r: Approval needed before a patient sees a specialist under some plans
Primary care often issues it.
w: A letter of thanks to a patient for choosing the hospital for the care of the family
A bill that a specialist sends to the primary care doctor for professional advice
A list of specialists that the hospital pays to advertise in the local news

q: What is an explanation of benefits (EOB)?
r: A statement from an insurer showing how a claim was processed
It shows what was paid and what the patient owes.
w: A bill from a doctor that asks the patient for payment before any care is given
A list of hospital departments, with the names of the managers and their phone numbers
A consent form that a patient signs before a surgery is carried out

q: What is capitation?
r: A payment of a fixed amount per patient per period regardless of services used
The provider bears the risk of costs.
w: A payment for each service performed on a patient by the clinic or the hospital
A payment made only after a patient has fully recovered from an illness or injury
A payment made by a patient to a hospital for the cost of a private room

q: What is fee-for-service?
r: Providers are paid for each service they perform
More services mean more payment.
w: Providers receive one fixed payment per patient each year, whatever services are used
Providers are paid only if the patient is cured within a set number of days
Providers are paid a salary by the government and bill nobody for their work

q: What is value-based care?
r: A payment approach that rewards providers for quality and outcomes
It aims to improve results while lowering cost.
w: A payment approach that rewards the most services performed, whatever the outcome
A payment approach that gives all patients the same care regardless of need
A payment approach in which the patient pays for care only after an operation

q: What is a superbill?
r: A form listing services provided, used to bill insurance
It carries codes and fees.
w: A very large hospital bill sent to the insurer for payment of a long stay
A bill that a patient receives after he has used up the benefits of his plan
A bill from a supplier to a hospital for the purchase of new equipment

q: What is a CMS-1500 form used for?
r: Billing insurers for services provided by physicians and suppliers
It is a standard claim form.
w: Admitting patients to a hospital, with a form that the doctor signs at the bedside
Recording the vital signs of a patient during a visit to a clinic
Ordering medicines from a pharmacy for the patients on a hospital ward

q: What is revenue cycle management?
r: Managing the process from patient registration through final payment
It aims to collect payment efficiently.
w: Managing hospital cafeteria menus, along with the food orders and the kitchen staff
Managing the supply of medicines in the hospital pharmacy and their prices
Managing the schedules of nurses and doctors on the wards of the hospital

q: What is a self-pay (cash) patient?
r: A patient who pays for services directly without using insurance
Cash prices may apply.
w: A patient whose employer pays the whole bill for care directly to the hospital
A patient whose care is paid for entirely by the government with no bill to the patient
A patient who pays in advance for a whole year of care in a single lump sum

q: What is accounts receivable in a healthcare organization?
r: Money owed to the provider for services already delivered
Payers and patients owe it.
w: Money the provider owes to suppliers for medicines and equipment bought on credit
Money the provider has in the bank and can spend on any purpose it wishes
Money the provider earns from investments in the stock market each year

q: What does 'days in accounts receivable' measure?
r: The average time it takes to collect payment after services
Lower numbers suggest faster collection.
w: The number of days that a patient stays in the hospital after an operation
The number of days that a supplier waits to be paid by the hospital for goods
The number of days between the time a patient books an appointment and the visit

q: A clinic has fixed costs of $20,000 a month and each visit brings in $100 with variable costs of $60. How many visits are needed to break even?
r: 500 visits
$20,000 divided by the $40 margin per visit.
w: 200 visits, found by dividing the fixed costs by the revenue earned from each visit
333 visits, found by dividing the fixed costs by the variable cost of each visit
The margin is revenue minus cost.
2,000 visits, found by multiplying the margin per visit by the fixed costs

q: A clinic's revenue for a month is $150,000 and its expenses are $140,000. What is the operating margin?
r: About 6.7 percent
w: About 10 percent, found by dividing the profit by the expenses of the clinic
About 93 percent, found by dividing the expenses by the revenue for the month
About 15 percent, found by dividing the revenue by the profit of the clinic

q: What is a revenue center in a hospital?
r: A department that generates income, such as radiology
It bills for services.
w: A department that only costs money, such as housekeeping or the billing office
A department that sets the price of every service in the hospital
A department that handles the complaints of patients and their families

q: What is a cost center in a hospital?
r: A department that incurs costs but does not directly bill patients, such as housekeeping
It supports other units.
w: A department that earns income by billing patients for the care it gives to them
A department that sets the budget for the whole of the hospital each year
A department that is closed because it costs more than it brings in

q: What is a capital budget in a hospital?
r: A plan for major, long-lasting purchases such as equipment or buildings
It covers items like an MRI machine.
w: A plan for monthly office supplies and other small purchases of the hospital
A plan for the salaries of staff and the bonuses of the executives of the hospital
That is part of operating costs.
A plan for the funds that the hospital keeps in a savings account for emergencies

q: What is an operating budget?
r: A plan for day-to-day revenues and expenses
It covers wages, supplies and utilities.
w: A plan for major, long-lasting purchases such as new buildings and large machines
A plan for how the hospital will spend the money from a single large donation
A plan for the number of beds that the hospital will have in ten years

q: What is a variance in budgeting?
r: The difference between budgeted and actual amounts
It flags where results differ from the plan.
w: A type of insurance plan that covers the losses of a hospital from a fire
A list of all the departments in a hospital and the names of their managers
A forecast of the number of patients who will visit the hospital next year

q: A department budgeted $50,000 for supplies and spent $55,000. What is the variance?
r: $5,000 unfavorable
Spending exceeded the budget.
w: $5,000 favorable, since the department spent more than it planned to spend
$105,000, found by adding the budget and the actual spending of the department
$0, since the actual spending is close to the budgeted amount for the period

q: What is a fixed cost in a hospital?
r: A cost that does not change with patient volume, such as building rent
It remains the same in the short run.
w: A cost that rises with each patient treated, such as medicines and dressings
A cost that is fixed by law and cannot be changed by the hospital's managers
A cost that the hospital pays only once, at the time that it opens its doors

q: What is a variable cost in a clinic?
r: A cost that changes with the number of patients, such as medical supplies
It rises and falls with volume.
w: A cost that stays the same regardless of the number of patients, such as rent
A cost that changes from month to month because of a mistake in the books
A cost that is paid by the patient directly to the supplier of the goods

q: What is cost containment?
r: Efforts to control and reduce healthcare spending without harming quality
Examples include bulk purchasing.
w: Increasing prices on all services so that the hospital can raise its yearly income
Cutting the number of staff to the minimum even if care becomes unsafe
Storing medical waste in sealed containers until it can be taken away

q: Which action best helps contain costs without hurting care quality?
r: Using bulk purchasing and reducing wasted supplies
Savings do not reduce care.
w: Delaying all equipment repairs until the machines have broken down completely
Hiring fewer nurses than are needed to care for the patients on the ward
Skipping safety checks on equipment to save the time of the technicians

q: What is a charge master?
r: A list of a provider's standard prices for services and items
Also called the chargemaster.
w: A manager who oversees credit cards for the hospital and reports to the finance office
A document that lists the amounts that insurers have agreed to pay for services
A report of the revenue that each department of the hospital earned in a year

q: Why do insurers often pay less than the amount billed?
r: They negotiate discounted rates with in-network providers
The allowed amount is below the charge.
w: Hospitals always overcharge on purpose, so the insurers must cut the bills they receive
Insurers are required by law to pay only half of every bill that they receive
Insurers pay less to punish patients who use their plan more than once a year

q: What does a hospital's governing board do?
r: Oversees the hospital's mission, policies and top leadership
It sets direction and holds executives accountable.
w: Schedules appointments at the front desk and answers the phone for the whole clinic
Treats patients in the wards and prescribes medicine for their illnesses
Cleans the rooms and halls of the hospital and keeps its grounds tidy

q: What is a nonprofit hospital?
r: A hospital that reinvests surplus revenue into its mission rather than paying owners
It may receive tax exemptions.
w: A hospital owned by investors who take profits and pay dividends to shareholders
A hospital that is not allowed to earn any income at all from the care it gives
A hospital that charges nothing to any patient for any kind of care it provides

q: What is a for-profit hospital?
r: A hospital owned by investors that aims to earn a profit
Profits may be paid to shareholders.
w: A hospital that reinvests all of its surplus in its mission and has no owners
A hospital that is run by a religious order only, with no aim of earning a profit
A hospital that is owned by the government and funded by taxes alone

q: What is a critical access hospital?
r: A small rural hospital with special Medicare payment rules
It helps keep rural care available.
w: A large urban trauma center with hundreds of beds and surgeons on call all day
A hospital that accepts only patients who have a very serious illness
A hospital that is open only in the summer months of the year

q: What is average length of stay (ALOS)?
r: The average number of days patients stay in the hospital
It is a measure of efficiency.
w: The wait time in the ER before a patient is seen by a doctor or a nurse
The average time a doctor spends with a patient during a single visit
The number of years that a hospital has been open to the public

q: What is a hospital readmission?
r: A patient returning to the hospital within a short time after discharge
Many are tracked within 30 days.
w: A patient's visit to the pharmacy for a refill of medicine that the doctor ordered
A patient who is admitted to the hospital for the first time in his life
A patient who is moved from one ward to another during the same stay

q: What is a 30-day readmission rate?
r: The share of patients readmitted within 30 days of discharge
It is a quality measure.
w: The share of patients admitted on holidays, compared with ordinary days
The share of patients who stay in the hospital for more than 30 days
The share of beds that are empty on the thirtieth day of the month

q: What is bed occupancy rate?
r: The share of available beds that are in use
Occupied beds divided by available beds.
w: The number of beds that the hospital builds in a given year
The number of patients who are admitted each day to the hospital
The price charged for a night in a hospital bed on a ward

q: A hospital has 200 beds and an average of 150 are occupied. What is its occupancy rate?
r: 75 percent
150 divided by 200.
w: 133 percent, found by dividing the total beds by the number of beds occupied
25 percent, which is the share of beds that are empty on an average day
50 percent, found by taking the average of the occupied and the empty beds

q: What is a deductible's effect on a patient's payments?
r: The patient pays the first part of covered costs before the plan pays
Higher deductibles lower premiums.
w: The plan pays the whole bill and the patient never pays anything toward the care
The patient pays a fee after the plan has paid its share of all the costs
The patient pays nothing until the end of the year, when a single bill is sent

q: What is bad debt in a hospital?
r: Revenue the hospital expected but could not collect from patients who could pay
It is a cost of billing.
w: Care that the hospital provides at no cost to patients who cannot afford to pay
Money the hospital owes to its suppliers for goods bought on credit
Loans from a bank that the hospital has repaid ahead of schedule

q: What is charity care?
r: Care provided at no or reduced cost to patients who cannot afford to pay
It is part of a hospital's community role.
w: Care paid for by insurers at a rate higher than the usual allowed amount
Care given only to hospital staff and their families free of charge
Care that a hospital bills in full but which the patient does not pay

q: What is an electronic health record (EHR)?
r: A digital version of a patient's medical history kept by providers
It can be shared across care settings.
w: A paper folder kept in a locked cabinet in the office of the family doctor
A bill sent to a patient after a visit to the hospital for care
A list of the staff who work in a hospital, along with their schedules

q: What is computerized provider order entry (CPOE)?
r: A system where clinicians enter orders such as medications electronically
It reduces errors from handwriting.
w: A system that schedules cleaning of the wards and the rooms for the hospital staff
A system that orders office supplies for the administrative staff each month
A system that bills patients for the cost of the meals served on the wards

q: What is a clinical decision support system?
r: Software that gives clinicians alerts and guidance to support decisions
It can flag drug interactions.
w: Software that replaces clinicians entirely, so that no human decisions are needed
Software that schedules the cleaning of rooms for the staff of a hospital
Software that prints bills and mails them to patients at the end of the month

q: What is interoperability?
r: The ability of different health IT systems to exchange and use information
It supports coordinated care.
w: The ability of a hospital to treat many patients at once in its emergency department
The ability of a doctor to work in several hospitals at the same time
The ability of a computer to run for many years without any need for repairs

q: What is a health information exchange (HIE)?
r: Secure sharing of patient information among healthcare organizations
It helps providers see a patient's records.
w: Posting health tips on social media for the public to read, share and comment upon
A market where patients buy and sell their used medical equipment to one another
A meeting where doctors swap stories about their patients with each other

q: What is a patient portal?
r: A secure website where patients view records and message providers
It supports patient engagement.
w: A door where patients enter the hospital, which is staffed by a team of guards
A computer in the waiting room that shows the news and the weather to visitors
A bill-paying machine in the lobby that takes cash and gives change to patients

q: What is telehealth?
r: Delivering healthcare services through video, phone or other technology
It extends access to care.
w: Delivering care only to elderly patients, who live in rural areas far from a hospital
Delivering medicines to patients' homes by drones controlled from a hospital
Delivering television programs about health to the rooms of patients in a hospital

q: Which patient benefits most from telehealth?
r: One living far from a clinic who needs a routine follow-up
Distance is removed as a barrier.
w: One who needs a broken bone set, since a physician must examine the limb in person
One who needs an emergency operation in an operating room as soon as possible
One who needs a blood test that can be done only in a laboratory at a hospital

q: What is remote patient monitoring?
r: Using technology to track a patient's health data from home
Devices send readings to providers.
w: Watching patients through hospital windows from the street outside the ward each day
Sending a nurse to visit a patient at home once a year to ask about their health
Recording a video of a patient's room and storing it in a locked cabinet

q: What does role-based access mean in a health information system?
r: Limiting system access to the information needed for a person's job
It protects patient privacy.
w: Access based on seniority only, so that the longest-serving staff see all records
Access granted to everyone in the hospital so that staff can find facts quickly
Access given only to the person who owns the largest number of shares

q: What is data backup in a healthcare setting?
r: Making copies of records so they can be restored if lost
It supports recovery from failure.
w: Moving records to an unsecured drive so that anyone on the staff can reach them
Deleting old records every night to free up space on the hospital's computers
Printing records on paper and storing them in boxes in an open hallway

q: What is the HIPAA Security Rule mainly about?
r: Safeguards for electronic protected health information
It sets administrative, physical and technical protections.
w: Security guards in parking lots, who watch the cars that belong to patients and staff
Rules about who may enter the hospital building at night and in the early morning
Rules about the locks on the doors of the pharmacy and of the supply rooms

q: What is protected health information (PHI)?
r: Individually identifiable health information held by covered entities
It includes records and billing data.
w: Public information about hospital prices and services, which is posted on the website
Information about the weather forecast for a city in the week ahead
Information about the sales of a pharmacy, grouped by product and by month

q: Which practice best protects patient data?
r: Use unique passwords and limit access to those who need it
Basic security habits reduce risk.
w: Leave screens open in public areas so that staff can reach records quickly when needed
Share a single password among all staff so that logins are easy to remember
Write passwords on notes stuck to monitors so that nobody forgets them

q: Two staff members discuss a patient's diagnosis in a crowded elevator. What is the problem?
r: A privacy breach risk, since others could overhear protected information
Discuss patients only where it is private.
w: Nothing wrong, because elevators are private spaces for staff and for no one else
The staff are not using enough medical words to describe the patient's condition
The elevator is too slow for the staff to finish the conversation in time

q: A caller asks about a family member's test results. What should the front desk do?
r: Verify authorization before sharing any information
Release only to permitted persons.
w: Share results with anyone who sounds worried on the phone about their relative
Share results with anyone who gives the name of the patient correctly
Share results with the caller in order to be polite and to save time

q: What is a medical record entry error corrected with?
r: Draw a single line through it, date and initial the correction
The original must stay readable.
w: Use correction fluid to hide it, so that the record looks clean and free of errors
Tear out the page and write a new one without telling the doctor or the nurse
Erase the entry completely and write the new one in the same place

q: What is e-prescribing?
r: Sending prescriptions electronically from the provider to a pharmacy
It reduces handwriting errors.
w: Printing a prescription on paper and handing it to the patient to take to a store
Selling medicines on a website without a prescription from any doctor
Storing old prescriptions in a computer file that no one is allowed to open

q: How does electronic prescribing help patient safety?
r: It reduces handwriting errors and can warn about drug interactions
The system checks orders.
w: It removes all need for pharmacists, since the computer fills every order by itself
It lets patients write their own prescriptions for the medicines they want
It sends the same prescription to all patients without checking their records

q: What is artificial intelligence used for in healthcare?
r: Supporting imaging analysis, risk prediction and administrative automation
Humans remain responsible for care.
w: Replacing all clinicians immediately, so that hospitals can run without any doctors
Deleting patient records that are older than one year from the systems of hospitals
Setting the price of medicines in the shops without any regulation

q: Which approach best helps a patient with low health literacy understand instructions?
r: Use plain language and ask the patient to repeat the plan back
Teach-back confirms understanding.
w: Hand over a long document without explaining it, so that the patient can read it later
Use medical terms to show the patient that the staff are well trained
Speak quickly so that the visit is short and the next patient can be seen

q: What is the teach-back method?
r: Asking patients to explain information in their own words to confirm understanding
It checks that instructions were understood.
w: Asking patients to teach the doctor medicine, so that the staff can learn from their stories
Giving patients a written test at the end of every visit to the clinic
Teaching patients about their health with a video that they watch alone

q: What does a chief medical officer (CMO) typically oversee?
r: Clinical quality and physician leadership
The CMO links medicine and administration.
w: Building construction and repairs, along with the upkeep of the grounds of the hospital
The hospital's investments and its relations with banks and lenders
The computer systems and networks that the hospital uses for records

q: What does a chief financial officer (CFO) do in a hospital?
r: Leads financial strategy, budgeting and reporting
Manages revenue and costs.
w: Leads the care of patients on the wards and decides which treatments are used
Leads the repair and upkeep of the buildings and equipment of the hospital
Leads the recruiting and training of nurses and other clinical staff

q: What is a department in a hospital?
r: A unit that focuses on a particular service, such as radiology or pharmacy
Each has its own staff and manager.
w: A building that is separate from the hospital, with its own address and staff
A group of patients who share the same insurance plan and the same doctor
A committee of doctors that meets once a year to review the hospital's budget

q: What does a pharmacy department do?
r: Prepares and dispenses medications and advises on their use
Pharmacists check orders for safety.
w: Performs surgery on patients in the operating rooms of the hospital each day

q: What does the prefix 'hyper-' mean?
r: Above normal or excessive
Hypertension is high blood pressure.

q: What does the prefix 'hypo-' mean?
r: Below normal or deficient
Hypoglycemia is low blood sugar.

q: What does the abbreviation 'BID' mean in a prescription?
r: Twice a day
From the Latin bis in die.

q: What does the abbreviation 'PRN' mean in a prescription?
r: As needed
Taken when required.

q: What does 'NPO' mean?
r: Nothing by mouth
Patients may not eat or drink.

q: What do vital signs usually include?
r: Temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure
They show basic body function.
w: Height, weight and shoe size, which are measured when a patient is first admitted
Name, address and insurance number of the patient
Allergies, past surgeries and family history of the patient

q: What does a blood pressure reading of 120/80 represent?
r: Systolic over diastolic pressure in mm Hg
The top number is pressure when the heart beats.
w: Pulse over respiration, measured in breaths per minute by the nurse at the bedside

q: What is a typical normal adult body temperature?
r: About 98.6°F
Around 37°C.
w: About 108°F, which is a little above what a doctor would call normal for a healthy adult

q: What is the first step in the patient check-in process?
r: Verifying identity and insurance information
This avoids errors and denials.
w: Discharging the patient, which is the last step after treatment is complete and the bill paid
Sending the final bill to the insurer before the visit
Taking the patient to the operating room

q: Why is it important to verify a patient's insurance at check-in?
r: To confirm coverage and avoid claim denials
Errors cause delays.
w: To avoid seeing the patient, since the front desk can then send the person away
To decide how much the doctor will charge the patient
To find out the patient's medical history

q: What is double-booking an appointment slot likely to cause?
r: Longer waits and rushed visits
Two patients compete for the same time.
w: Shorter waits for everyone who is on the schedule that day
Fewer errors in the records of the patients

q: What is a no-show?
r: A patient who misses an appointment without canceling
It wastes a time slot.
w: A patient who cancels days ahead, so that the slot can be given to another person
A patient who arrives early for a visit
A patient who is seen by the wrong doctor

q: Which practice helps reduce no-shows?
r: Sending appointment reminders
Reminders raise attendance.
w: Scheduling without telling the patient the date and time of the visit to the clinic
Making appointments weeks later than patients ask for

q: What is a numeric filing system?
r: Records filed by number
Each record has an assigned number.
w: Records filed by color, with a different shade of folder used for each customer
Records filed alphabetically by the last name of the patient
Records filed by the date on which the patient was born

q: What is the SOAP note format?
r: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
A structure for charting.
w: Staff, Office, Admin and Policy, the four headings used in hospital management

q: What is the purpose of appointment scheduling?
r: To organize patient visits efficiently and reduce waiting
It balances provider time.
w: To avoid seeing patients who call the office and ask for visits on busy days
To raise the fees of the clinic
To keep patients out of the building

q: What is a patient chart?
r: A record of a patient's health history, treatment and notes
It supports continuity of care.
w: A list of staff schedules posted in the nurses' station for the week ahead
A chart of the weather for the week
A diagram of the hospital rooms

q: What is a medical necessity?
r: Services that are reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition
Insurers pay for necessary care.
w: Services offered for convenience only, which the patient requests but the doctor does not order
Services that a patient wants but which have no medical basis
Services offered to staff as a perk of the job

q: What is a statistic that shows how long patients wait to be seen?
r: Wait time
It measures access.
w: Occupancy rate, which is the share of beds in use at the hospital
Readmission rate, which counts patients returning after discharge
Length of stay, which measures days spent in the hospital

q: What does a health unit coordinator do?
r: Manages communication and paperwork on a hospital unit
It supports nursing staff.
w: Performs laboratory tests on blood and tissue samples taken from patients on the unit
Performs surgery on patients in the operating rooms of the hospital
Prescribes drugs to patients after a short examination

q: What is HIPAA-compliant disposal of paper records?
r: Shredding or securely destroying documents containing patient information
It prevents exposure.
w: Throwing them in the regular trash bins behind the clinic, where waste is collected each week
Leaving them in a pile in a hallway until someone collects them
Giving them to a patient's neighbor to throw away

q: What is a superbill used for?
r: Listing services provided so that insurance can be billed
It carries the codes.
w: Telling a patient what the doctor ate for lunch
